name: Zapatismo
summary: Zapatismo is the agrarian revolutionary outlook of Emiliano Zapata and the Liberation Army of the South in the Mexican Revolution. It held that land, water and woods taken by haciendas must be restored to the villages and that great estates must be broken up so every family can farm its own plot, communally or as small property. Around that core its intellectuals drafted a social state: recognition of unions and strikes, labour protections, public assistance as justice, municipal self-government, popular juries, plebiscites on laws and an armed people in place of a standing army.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: The Zapatista agrarian law recognises communal and small private ownership and leaves communities and individuals free to choose between them (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter 'El Consejo Ejecutivo de la República', p. 260).

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Zapatista public-assistance law condemned charity as degrading and contrary to equality, and made the state, through the municipalities, provide meals, shelter, clothing and free medical care in its place (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, pp. 262-263).

civil-marriage.rationale: The Zapatista marriage law recognised civil marriage and free union as legitimate with equal legal standing (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 268).

collective-farming.rationale: The Zapatista agrarian law puts communal and individual small holdings on equal legal footing and respects each community's and individual's free choice of regime, so it does not replace individual farms with collective ones (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 260).

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) condemns Madero for imposing a vice-president and governors against the people's will and for making effective suffrage a trick, and provides for elections after victory.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: A Zapatista law proposed the immediate abolition of taxes on articles of prime necessity (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 268).

death-penalty.rationale: Mendoza López's Zapatista justice law abolished the death penalty for ever (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 265).

decide-locally.rationale: Zapatista programmes made the municipalities and local juntas the bodies that carry out and watch over land and labour reforms, and the Convention programme included municipal independence, though the ministries planned centrally (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, pp. 260-264).

democracy-best.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls for elections to federal and state powers after victory, and the council held that real democracy means voters approve laws as well as choose rulers.

direct-action.rationale: The Plan of Ayala tells villages to take immediate possession of stolen land, rather than wait for courts or legislatures, though it also planned elections.

direct-votes.rationale: The Zapatista plebiscite law said the fundamental laws of the Republic must be ratified by the people's vote, since democracy means approving or rejecting laws as well as electing representatives (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 269).

elective-rulers.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) has an interim president and the governors call elections to organise the federal and state powers, and condemns imposed appointments such as Figueroa's.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The public-assistance law rejected charity as contrary to 'the equality of all men', and Zapata's letter speaks for all oppressed humanity.

gradual-change.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls Mexicans to take up arms, seize stolen lands at once and accept no compromise with the old regime.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Plan of Ayala breaks with Madero precisely because a political revolution without land reform was a betrayal; land was the cause of the revolution.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The Plan of Ayala restores land, woods and water to villages holding title to them, many of them Nahua communities that had held land in common.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The agrarian law recognised the rights of communities as well as individuals to restored land and to choose communal tenure.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) orders a third of the monopolised estates expropriated, and non-cooperating landlords' goods nationalised, so villages and citizens get ejidos and fields; the Zapatista agrarian law (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter 'El Consejo Ejecutivo de la República', pp. 259-261) expropriates the estates of the revolution's enemies to give every family land.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Zapata called land the property of all, and the movement's motto was that land belongs to those who work it.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: An armed movement, Zapatismo told villages to defend recovered land by force of arms.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The Zapatista marriage law recognised the right to divorce at the request of the parties (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 268).

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Montaño's Zapatista education law made primary schooling free and secular, provided by the federation, states and municipalities (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 268).

participatory-democracy.rationale: Zapatista proposals gave ordinary people direct roles: elected municipal Juntas de Reformas that settle land and labour cases, popular juries, and plebiscites on the fundamental laws (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, pp. 262-265, 269).

people-in-arms.rationale: The Zapatista law on the permanent army called it an instrument of murder used by governments to oppress the people and put the armed people in its place, with police forces for peace-time security (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, pp. 267-268).

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Plan of Ayala denounces Madero as a traitor allied with the old científicos, and the council required officials to be watched by the people and barred from enriching themselves.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) takes up arms against Madero and tells Mexicans to support the plan with arms in hand; the pueblos are to hold restored lands by arms.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Zapata blamed poverty on the monopoly of land by 'a few powerful individuals', and Mendoza López on landlords' rent.

positive-liberty.rationale: Zapatismo held that freedom required land for subsistence: the agrarian law made the state guarantee each person's natural right to the land they need.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Zapatista intellectuals' social state was to direct national development and serve first the most numerous and unprotected classes, after a broad land reform (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, conclusion, p. 270).

property-fundamental.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) overrides landlords' title by restitution and expropriation, and nationalises opponents' property; only small property is protected (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 260).

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Zapata's 1918 letter (s2) calls land, like water and air, the property of all, wrongly monopolised by a few, and the Plan de Ayala (s1) takes back land, timber and water that monopolies hold.

rehabilitation.rationale: The Zapatista justice law held society to blame for crime and made the state responsible for regenerating offenders in agricultural and industrial centres, not for punishing them (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 265).

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) strips Madero of recognition for disregarding the Constitution of 1857, the law and the people's rights, and rises in arms against him.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) pledges to defend its principles 'until victory or death' and rejects any compromise with the dictatorial powers.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Zapatista delegates in the Convention pushed through legal recognition of the right to strike and of boycott and sabotage against the northern delegates' opposition (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 261).

revolution-legitimate.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) disowns Madero, calls on the people to support it 'with arms in hand' and declares the revolution continued until the dictatorial powers are overthrown.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) condemns Madero for contempt of the law and justice of the pueblos and for violating the prior laws of the 1857 code.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The Zapatista law on the permanent army said force resides in the social collectivity and that the armed people replaces the standing army, which ends the state's monopoly of arms (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 267).

state-harmful.rationale: The Zapatista intellectuals worked to build a new 'social state' for the working classes, with ministries of agriculture, labour and justice (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, conclusion, p. 270).

strong-leader.rationale: The Plan of Ayala declares its authors 'partisans of principles and not of men' and repudiates Madero's personal rule, rejecting a leader above the law.

term-limits.rationale: The movement upheld the revolutionary principle of no reelection that the Plan of Ayala accuses Madero of betraying.

unions-good.rationale: Zapatista delegates in the Convention won the vote to recognise workers' associations, the right to strike, the boycott and sabotage in its programme (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter, p. 261).

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The Plan de Ayala (s1) names 'Effective Suffrage and No Reelection' as sacred principles that Madero betrayed.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Zapata wrote that land monopolised by a few powerful individuals, backed by armies and laws, had kept peasants exploited for generations.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The Zapatista agrarian law gives communal land and small private property equal legal standing, caps small holdings at 100-1,000 hectares and gives tenants and sharecroppers ownership of what they farm (s6, Ávila Espinosa chapter 'El Consejo Ejecutivo de la República', pp. 260-261); the Plan de Ayala (s1) seeks fields, colonies and ejidos for the many.

worker-farmer-alliance.rationale: Zapata's 1918 letter (s2) says the worker's emancipation cannot be won unless the peasant is freed too, and urges workers and peasants to carry out the two tasks jointly.

workers-nation.rationale: Zapata's 1918 letter (s2) ties the Mexican land revolution to the Russian one and says the international proletariat will support it, urging worker solidarity across borders.

missingStatements.text: Land, water and woods taken from villages by large estates should be restored to the villages.
missingStatements.rationale: Restitution of usurped village lands under their old titles is the first demand of the Plan of Ayala and the core of the 1915 Agrarian Law.

scope: Zapatismo as Mexican historians define it (Ávila, s4; Crespo, s6; INEHRM, s5): the agrarian revolutionary movement that grew around Emiliano Zapata and the Anenecuilco leaders in Morelos and neighbouring states during the Mexican Revolution (1910-1919), with its programme in the Plan de Ayala (s1) and the intellectuals' later social and political proposals (Montaño, Palafox, Díaz Soto y Gama). Its core is the restoration of village lands, water and woods and the breaking up of the haciendas, with village self-government. The later Chiapas movement of the EZLN (neo-Zapatismo) is a separate subject and is not part of this scope.
